structured_output.hypothesis: In sunflower capitula, the two families of conspicuous contact parastichy spirals cross at angles that are not clustered at 90 degrees, so orthogonal crossing is the exception.
structured_output.pass_criterion: From floret-centre coordinates or segmented images of at least 30 capitula, measure the local crossing angle between the two nearest-neighbour parastichy families at each floret. The claim passes if fewer than 25% of florets, pooled over capitula, have crossing angles within 90±5 degrees. It must also pass on the per-capitulum measure: the median per-capitulum fraction within 90±5 degrees is below 25%. Finally, the angle must be roughly constant along each spiral, meaning the within-capitulum coefficient of variation of crossing angle is below 0.15 outside the central 10% of the radius.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim fails if 50% or more of florets, or the median capitulum, have crossing angles within 90±5 degrees. It also fails if the crossing angle varies systematically with radius by more than 20% (coefficient of variation above 0.30), because that would mean the spirals are not isogonal.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'spirals' are the visible contact parastichies, treated as logarithmic spirals about a common pole. 'Isogonal' means a constant crossing angle along the spiral, which is the defining property of a logarithmic spiral. 'Orthogonal' means a 90 degree crossing, which Church argued for. Modern reinterpretation: sunflower capitula follow Vogel's model, with a divergence angle near 137.5 degrees and florets at radius proportional to the square root of their index. Parastichy crossing angles are therefore known to approach 90 degrees in the outer capitulum, and they vary with radius near the centre, where they are not constant. A real test must therefore measure per-floret angles, not assume a model. The claim is stated for sunflowers generally, so it is not weakened to a single capitulum or a single radius band.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: I could not identify, and so could not verify, any public dataset of sunflower floret coordinates or parastichy crossing angles with a resolvable landing page or DOI. The portals I know well (GBIF, NCBI, Dryad, Zenodo, figshare) hold sunflower genomes, occurrence records and agronomic phenotyping data. None is a confirmed record of per-floret positions or spiral crossing angles. Naming one from memory would risk a fabricated identifier. The test needs a new capitulum image set with floret segmentation, or a floret-coordinate deposit from a phyllotaxis study.
